mainTopic: A gentile's residence in a shared courtyard, the practical ruling like רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, and the ban on a student ruling in his teacher's place
overview: The גמרא examines a ברייתא that says a gentile's courtyard is like an animal pen. It asks why our משנה says a gentile in a shared courtyard does prohibit carrying. The answer is that a gentile prohibits only when he is present. Then the גמרא asks what principle explains why an absent Jew prohibits but an absent gentile does not. It answers that a home without its owner (דירה בלא בעלים) does not count. The רבנן decreed that an absent Jew still prohibits. A gentile prohibits even when present only because of a גזירה, so no further decree was added for when he is away. A משנה about a gentile who left town is explained as a case where he returns on שבת itself. The גמרא then rules like רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, with three levels of strength: הלכה, מנהג, or נהגו העם. This leads to a discussion of whether a student may rule in his teacher's place. רב חסדא would not rule even on an egg in כותח during רב הונא's lifetime, but he did rule in the town of כפרי.

steps.title: Quoting the ruling that a gentile's courtyard is like an animal pen
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings back a line from the ברייתא it quoted earlier: a gentile's courtyard is like an animal pen.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: The courtyard of a gentile is like the pen of an animal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting a line from the ברייתא it cited earlier so that it can examine it. This sets up the challenge that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An animal pen is not a human home, so it does not prohibit carrying. Comparing a gentile's courtyard to an animal pen means that a gentile's home does not count as a real residence for the laws of עירוב.

keyTerms.meaning: "The Master said". This phrase brings back an earlier quoted source so it can be analyzed.
A gentile's courtyard
An animal pen. It is not a human residence.

phrases.english: The Master said:
phrases.notes: This refers back to the ברייתא cited earlier.

phrases.english: The courtyard of a gentile
is like the pen of an animal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This step opens the analysis of a ברייתא that was quoted earlier on the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A gentile's courtyard does not count as a residence, so it does not prohibit carrying.

steps.title: Challenge from the משנה that a gentile does prohibit
steps.stepSummary: Our משנה says that someone living in a courtyard with a gentile is prohibited from carrying. That seems to contradict the ברייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't we learn in the משנה: One who lives with a gentile in a courtyard, the gentile prohibits him from carrying!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא by pointing to our משנה, which says the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says a gentile's home is like an animal pen and does not prohibit. The משנה says a gentile in a shared courtyard does prohibit carrying. These two sources seem to clash head-on.

keyTerms.meaning: "But didn't we learn?" This introduces a challenge from a משנה.
He prohibits carrying for him.
Gentile

phrases.english: But didn't we learn in the Mishnah:
One who lives with a gentile in a courtyard
this one prohibits him!
phrases.notes: The gentile prohibits the Jew from carrying.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This step attacks the ברייתא quoted in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's rule that a gentile's courtyard is like an animal pen
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה treats a gentile's residence as significant enough to prohibit carrying. That contradicts the ברייתא calling it an animal pen.

steps.title: The gentile is present versus away
steps.stepSummary: The משנה is talking about a gentile who is home. The ברייתא is talking about a gentile who is away.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is not difficult. The משנה is where the gentile is present. The ברייתא is where he is not present.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא resolves the contradiction by assigning each source to a different situation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the gentile is physically there, he prohibits carrying, as the משנה says. When he is away, his courtyard is like an empty animal pen and does not prohibit, as the ברייתא says. So the two sources do not really argue.

keyTerms.meaning: "It is not difficult." This introduces a resolution.
Where he is present
Where he is not present

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two "הָא"s. The first one (דְּאִיתֵיהּ, present) goes with the משנה, which prohibits. The second one (דְּלֵיתֵיהּ, away) goes with the ברייתא, which permits.

phrases.english: It is not difficult:
This is where he is present.
phrases.notes: This refers to the משנה. A gentile who is present prohibits.

phrases.english: That is where he is not present.
phrases.notes: This refers to the ברייתא. A gentile who is away does not prohibit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This step answers the challenge in step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing cases (אוקימתא): each source refers to a different situation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The sources seemed to argue about whether a gentile's residence counts at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: A gentile who is present prohibits. A gentile who is away does not.

steps.title: What principle explains treating an absent Jew and an absent gentile differently?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the ברייתא's author (רבי מאיר) holds about a home without its owner. Either answer seems to cause a problem.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does he hold? If he holds that a home without its owner still counts as a home, then even an absent gentile should prohibit. If he holds that a home without its owner does not count as a home, then even an absent Jew should not prohibit!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up a two-sided problem. Neither possible principle seems to fit the ruling that an absent Jew prohibits but an absent gentile does not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is about דירה בלא בעלים, a home whose owner is away. If such a home counts, the gentile's home should count too. If it does not count, the Jew's home should not count either. Treating the two differently needs an explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: "And what does he hold?" This asks for the reasoning behind a view.
A residence without its owners present
It is considered a residence.
He should prohibit.

phrases.english: And what does he hold?
If he holds that a residence without owners
is considered a residence,
then even a gentile should also prohibit.
And if he holds that a residence without owners
is not considered a residence,
then even a Jew should also not prohibit!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This step probes the principle behind the distinction made in step 3 and the ruling that an absent Jew prohibits.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that treats an absent Jew and an absent gentile differently
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: This is a dilemma. Whichever way the principle of דירה בלא בעלים goes, the Jew and the gentile should be treated the same.

steps.title: A home without its owner does not count, but the רבנן decreed about a Jew
steps.stepSummary: A home without its owner is not a real home. However, the רבנן decreed that an absent Jew still prohibits, because a Jew prohibits when he is present.
steps.simpleTranslation: Actually, he holds that a home without its owner is not considered a home. But a Jew, who prohibits when he is present, was the subject of a Rabbinic decree: even when he is away, he prohibits.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the basic principle is that an empty home does not count. The Jew is different only because of a Rabbinic גזירה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By the basic rule, neither an absent Jew nor an absent gentile would prohibit. The רבנן extended the Jew's present-day prohibition to times when he is away, perhaps so people would not confuse the two situations. They did not make a similar extension for the gentile.

keyTerms.meaning: "Actually". This introduces the true position after a dilemma.
The Rabbis made a decree about him.
He prohibits.

steps.whatToRemember: A home without its owner (דירה בלא בעלים) is not considered a home. An absent gentile does not prohibit carrying. An absent Jew does prohibit, but only because of a rabbinic גזירה, since he prohibits when he is present.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how the רבנן sometimes extend a rule beyond its basic logic through a גזירה. That explains why two cases that look the same on the surface are treated differently.

phrases.english: Actually, he holds

phrases.aramaic: דִּירָה בְּלֹא בְּעָלִים — לֹא שְׁמָהּ דִּירָה.
phrases.english: that a residence without owners is not considered a residence.
But a Jew, who prohibits when he is present,
when he is not present, the Rabbis made a decree regarding him.
phrases.notes: The decree is that he prohibits even when he is away.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This step resolves the dilemma raised in step 4.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Picking one side of the dilemma and explaining the exception through a Rabbinic decree
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The Jew and the gentile must follow the same principle about an absent owner.
steps.terutzMaskana: By the basic rule, an empty home does not count. The absent Jew prohibits only because of a גזירה, since he prohibits when he is present. No such decree was made for a gentile.

steps.title: A gentile who is away does not prohibit
steps.stepSummary: This finishes the previous answer. A gentile prohibits only because of a גזירה, so there is no extra decree when he is away.
steps.simpleTranslation: But a gentile, who even when he is home prohibits only because of a decree that the Jew might learn from his ways: when he is home, he prohibits; when he is not home, he does not prohibit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its answer by explaining why a gentile is different from a Jew. A gentile who is away does not prohibit carrying.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A Jew prohibits carrying when he is home by the basic law, so the רבנן also made him prohibit when he is away. A gentile prohibits even when he is home only because of a rabbinic decree, made so the Jew would not come to live with him and learn his ways. The רבנן did not stack a second decree on top of that first one, so an absent gentile does not prohibit.

keyTerms.meaning: A rabbinic decree made to protect against a problem
Lest he learn from his ways
When he is present (at home)
When he is not present (away)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think a gentile and a Jew prohibit for the same reason. A Jew prohibits by the basic law of residence. A gentile prohibits even when present only because of a גזירה (his residence on its own is 'like an animal pen'). That is why the רבנן did not extend his prohibition to when he is away.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a common pattern: the רבנן usually do not make a decree to protect another decree.

phrases.english: A gentile, who even when he is present —
phrases.notes: Contrasted with the Jew from the previous step.

phrases.english: it is only a decree lest one learn from his ways.
phrases.notes: The prohibition is there to stop a Jew from living near a gentile.

phrases.english: When he is present, he prohibits;
when he is not present, he does not prohibit.

steps.triggerLanguage: גּוֹי, דְּכִי אִיתֵיהּ גְּזֵירָה שֶׁמָּא יִלְמַד מִמַּעֲשָׂיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the תירוץ of step 5 by contrasting the gentile with the Jew.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction based on the source of the prohibition (a Jew prohibits under the basic law of עירוב חצרות, while a gentile prohibits only because of an extra גזירה; the רבנן do not add a גזירה on top of a גזירה)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: One might think a gentile who is away should prohibit just like a Jew who is away.
steps.terutzMaskana: A gentile prohibits only because of a decree, so no further decree applies when he is away.

steps.title: Challenge from a משנה about someone who left town
steps.stepSummary: A משנה says that רבי מאיר holds even a gentile who left town prohibits, which contradicts the previous step.
steps.simpleTranslation: And when he is not present, he does not prohibit? But we learned in a משנה: One who leaves his house and goes to spend שבת in another town, whether a gentile or a Jew, prohibits. These are the words of רבי מאיר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the claim that an absent gentile does not prohibit, using a משנה that says he does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer we just heard was given in the name of רבי מאיר's view. But in this משנה רבי מאיר himself says that a gentile who went away to another town still prohibits. That directly contradicts the rule that an absent gentile does not prohibit.

keyTerms.meaning: But did we not learn in a משנה?
One who leaves his house
To spend שבת in a different town
Prohibits (makes it forbidden for the others to carry)

phrases.english: And when he is not present, he does not prohibit?
phrases.notes: A question that works as a challenge.

phrases.english: But we learned in a Mishnah:
One who leaves his house and goes away
to spend Shabbat in another town,
whether a gentile or a Jew, he prohibits,
phrases.notes: The others in the courtyard may not carry.

phrases.english: these are the words of Rabbi Meir.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the rule from step 6 using a משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that, according to רבי מאיר, an absent gentile does not prohibit.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי מאיר explicitly says in a משנה that a gentile who left town still prohibits.

steps.title: The משנה is about someone returning the same day
steps.stepSummary: The משנה is talking about someone who will come back on שבת itself, so he prohibits even before he returns.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, it is a case where he comes back on that same day.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The משנה is about a person who will return on שבת itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the gentile will come back during שבת, then he will prohibit once he is home. So he already prohibits now, even before he arrives. Our rule that an absent gentile does not prohibit is about someone who will not return until after שבת.

keyTerms.meaning: There (in that other source)
Who comes back on that same day

phrases.english: There, it is where he comes back on that same day.
phrases.notes: He will return during Shabbat, so he prohibits even now.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the קשיא of step 7 by narrowing the case of the משנה.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to say that any absent gentile prohibits.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a gentile who will return during שבת prohibits. One who returns after שבת does not.

steps.title: How strongly we follow רבי אליעזר בן יעקב
steps.stepSummary: Three אמוראים agree we follow רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, but they disagree on how strongly: full הלכה, a מנהג, or only what the people already do.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: The הלכה follows רבי אליעזר בן יעקב. And רב הונא said: The מנהג follows רבי אליעזר בן יעקב. And רבי יוחנן said: The people are accustomed to follow רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now gives the practical ruling for the משנה's argument. All three opinions follow רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, who holds that a gentile does not prohibit unless two Jews live with him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The three opinions differ in strength. According to רב יהודה in the name of שמואל, it is full הלכה and is taught publicly. According to רב הונא, it is a מנהג, so a חכם rules this way only if asked. According to רבי יוחנן, the people already do it, so a חכם would not rule this way even if asked, but he would not protest either.

keyTerms.meaning: The binding ruling, taught publicly
A custom; ruled this way only for someone who asks
The people are accustomed; not ruled, but not protested
The תנא who holds that a gentile does not prohibit unless two Jews live there

steps.whatToRemember: In practice we follow רבי אליעזר בן יעקב. The only argument is how strongly: הלכה, מנהג, or נהגו העם.
steps.confusionAlert: These three are not arguing about what the law is. They all follow רבי אליעזר בן יעקב. They only argue about how publicly a חכם should teach it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the classic three-level scale of הלכה, מנהג, and נהגו העם, which appears in other places in ש״ס as well.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel:
The halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
phrases.notes: Taught publicly.

phrases.english: And Rav Huna said:
The custom follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
phrases.notes: Ruled this way only for someone who asks.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: נָהֲגוּ הָעָם כְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב.
phrases.english: The people are accustomed to follow Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
phrases.notes: Not ruled even if asked, but not protested.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from analyzing רבי מאיר's view to giving the practical ruling on the מחלוקת in the משנה.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: We follow רבי אליעזר בן יעקב: a gentile in the courtyard does not prohibit unless two Jews live there. The three opinions differ only on whether this is הלכה, מנהג, or נהגו העם.

steps.title: אביי states that the הלכה follows רבי אליעזר בן יעקב
steps.stepSummary: אביי reminds רב יוסף of two facts: the teachings of רבי אליעזר בן יעקב are always followed, and שמואל ruled like him in this case too.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רב יוסף: We hold that the teaching of רבי אליעזר בן יעקב is small in amount but clean. Also, רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: the הלכה follows רבי אליעזר בן יעקב.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי lays down a premise: the הלכה here is certain and clear. This is setting up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying "קב ונקי" means his teachings are few but always accepted as הלכה. With שמואל's ruling added, nobody doubts the הלכה. So the only question is not what the הלכה is, but who is allowed to say it.

keyTerms.meaning: We hold / it is established for us
The teaching of
A small measure, but clean. Few teachings, but all accepted as הלכה
The הלכה follows (so-and-so)

phrases.english: Abaye said to Rav Yosef:
phrases.notes: רב יוסף was אביי's teacher.

phrases.aramaic: קַיְימָא לַן מִשְׁנַת רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן יַעֲקֹב
phrases.english: We hold that the teaching of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
is a kav, but clean,
phrases.notes: A small amount of teachings, but the הלכה always follows them.

phrases.english: And Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel:
The halacha follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
phrases.notes: Here, in the case of the gentile and the עירוב.

steps.alternativePossibleLabel: שאלה (as the opening part of the question)
steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי לְרַב יוֹסֵף: קַיְימָא לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the conclusion of step 9 that we follow רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, and makes clear the הלכה is certain.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The הלכה clearly follows רבי אליעזר בן יעקב, both as a general rule and in this case.

steps.title: May a student rule in his teacher's place?
steps.stepSummary: Since the הלכה is so clear, may a student give this ruling in a place where his teacher is the authority?
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the law about giving a ruling in the place of one's teacher?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי asks whether a student may announce even a clear, accepted הלכה in his teacher's area.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a student may not rule in his teacher's place, because that is disrespectful to the teacher. אביי wonders whether a ruling this obvious is different, since the student is not really deciding anything new.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the law?
To give a halachic ruling
In the place of his teacher, where the teacher is the authority

phrases.english: What is the law about ruling in the place of one's teacher?
phrases.notes: Even on a הלכה that is completely clear.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the clear halacha from step 10 to ask about the rule of respecting one's teacher.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the ban on ruling in a teacher's place applies even to a clear, well-known הלכה.

steps.title: רב חסדא would not rule even on a simple egg question
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף answers no: רב חסדא would not rule even on an egg cooked in a dairy dish for as long as רב הונא was alive.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Even about an egg in כותח, they asked רב חסדא all the years of רב הונא, and he did not give a ruling.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף answers אביי's question with a story about רב חסדא and his teacher רב הונא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An egg in כותח (a dairy dish) is a very simple question, and the answer is obvious. Still, רב חסדא refused to answer it while his teacher רב הונא was alive. So a student may not rule in his teacher's place, even on the simplest and clearest matter.

keyTerms.meaning: An egg
כותח, a dip that contains milk
They asked him
And he did not give a ruling

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets a strong rule of respect: how simple the question is does not matter. In his teacher's place, during the teacher's lifetime, the student does not rule.

phrases.english: He said to him: Even about an egg in kutach
phrases.notes: An egg in a dairy dish, an easy and obvious question.

phrases.english: they asked Rav Chisda
all the years of Rav Huna,
phrases.notes: All the years רב הונא, his teacher, was alive.

phrases.english: and he did not give a ruling.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No. A student may not rule in his teacher's place even on the simplest matter, as shown by רב חסדא.

steps.title: What about rulings written openly for everyone to see?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יעקב בר אבא asks אביי whether a student may rule in his teacher's place on laws written in מגילת תענית, which anyone can read.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יעקב בר אבא said to אביי: For example, מגילת תענית, which is written and lying there. What is the law about ruling on it in the place of one's teacher?
steps.whatsHappening: A new person asks the same kind of question with a stronger case: laws that are already written down and available to everyone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מגילת תענית lists the days when fasting is forbidden, and it is written and open to all. The idea is that repeating something written is not really ruling, only reading. So perhaps a student may say it even in his teacher's place.

keyTerms.meaning: For example / such as
A scroll listing the days on which fasting is forbidden
That is written and lying there, open to all
In his teacher's place

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב בַּר אַבָּא לְאַבָּיֵי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yaakov bar Abba said to Abaye:
For example, Megillat Taanit,
phrases.notes: The list of days when fasting is forbidden.

phrases.english: which is written and lying there.
phrases.notes: Anyone can look it up.

phrases.english: What is the law about ruling in his teacher's place?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב בַּר אַבָּא לְאַבָּיֵי: כְּגוֹן מְגִלַּת תַּעֲנִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks the same question again about a stronger case: a law that is written and public, not just well known.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a written, public law may be stated by a student in his teacher's place.

steps.title: אביי answers with רב יוסף's same story
steps.stepSummary: אביי quotes רב יוסף's story about רב חסדא and the egg. Even written laws may not be ruled on in the teacher's place.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: רב יוסף said this: Even about an egg in כותח, they asked רב חסדא all the years of רב הונא, and he did not give a ruling.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers by repeating the exact story he himself had heard from his teacher רב יוסף.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same answer covers the new case. Even when a law is written for all to see, the student still does not rule in his teacher's place. אביי simply passes on his teacher רב יוסף's answer to the new question.

keyTerms.meaning: Thus said, quoting a teacher's words
All the years of (someone's lifetime)

steps.whatToRemember: A student may not give a ruling in הלכה in his teacher's place. This holds even when the הלכה is clear, simple, and even written down, as with רב חסדא, who would not rule on an egg in כותח during רב הונא's lifetime.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ, הָכִי אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף:
phrases.english: He said to him: Thus said Rav Yosef:
phrases.notes: אביי quotes his own teacher.

phrases.english: Even about an egg in kutach
they asked Rav Chisda
all the years of Rav Huna,
and he did not give a ruling.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ, הָכִי אָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 13 by repeating the answer from step 12.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: No. Even laws that are written and public may not be ruled on by a student in his teacher's place.

steps.title: רב חסדא ruled in כפרי during רב הונא's lifetime
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא gave halachic rulings in כפרי while רב הונא was still alive. This shows a student may rule outside his teacher's area.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא gave halachic rulings in the town of כפרי during the years when רב הונא was alive.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports a fact: רב חסדא did give rulings while רב הונא was alive, but only in a different town, כפרי. This sets the limit on the story we just heard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 12 and 14 said רב חסדא would not rule even on an egg while רב הונא lived. This report seems to clash with that, but it really narrows it. The ban covers ruling in the teacher's own place, and כפרי was a different town, outside רב הונא's place of authority, so ruling there was allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: Gave a ruling in הלכה (from הוֹרָאָה)
כפרי, a town in בבל, outside רב הונא's place of authority
In the years of / during the lifetime of

steps.whatToRemember: A student may not rule in the place where his teacher is the authority. But in a different place, outside his teacher's area, he may rule even while his teacher is alive.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this as a contradiction of the egg story. Both are true: in רב הונא's area רב חסדא held back completely, and in כפרי he ruled freely.
steps.whyThisMatters: It defines the scope of the איסור of הוראה בפני רבו. The ban depends on place (where the teacher is the authority), not only on time (the teacher's lifetime).

phrases.english: Rav Chisda issued rulings in Kafri
phrases.notes: כפרי was a separate town, outside רב הונא's local authority.

phrases.english: during the years of Rav Huna.
phrases.notes: That is, while רב הונא was still alive.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב חִסְדָּא אוֹרִי בְּכַפְרִי בִּשְׁנֵי דְּרַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Narrows the רב חסדא and egg story from steps 12 and 14: holding back applied only in רב הונא's own area, not in a distant town.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A student may give rulings during his teacher's lifetime when he is in a different place, outside the teacher's area of authority.
